newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Peace talks provoke more war in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Peace talks provoke more war in Tajikistan.

text.p: When peace talks between Tajikistan's shaky government and the Islamist opposition were announced last week, few observers were surprised when fighting flared in the former Soviet republic.

Diplomats and Russian officers belonging to the large Russian military contingent propping up the Tajik government said the upsurge in violence came from both sides' desire to beef up their bargaining position at the negotiating table.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov is supposed to meet opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri somewhere in northern Afghanistan on December 9.
"The trust factor is so low, it's hard to see how there will be any meaningful negotiations," said a Western diplomat in Dushanbe.
After fierce fighting on Sunday, Islamist guerrillas said they captured the town of Garm, 200 km (130 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe, from the government.

The fighting followed hard on the heels of two attacks killing Russian servicemen in Dushanbe, widely held to be the work of the increasingly confident opposition. One guerrilla band now operates only 13 km (9 miles) east of the capital.
"These talks are only going to mean more attacks," said a Russian officer based in the Tajik capital. "The opposition want to show that the government cannot control Dushanbe."

Tajik government troops, backed by the Russian military, have fought the Islamist opposition in the former Soviet republic for nearly five years in a bitter civil war which has cost tens of thousands of lives and displaced many more.
The opposition now controls the mountainous and sparsely populated eastern half of the country.
They are moving slowly but surely westwards towards Dushanbe where there is a palpable increase in tension.
"There are extra patrols and there is a larger military presence in the city so something's afoot," said one experienced aid worker living in the city.
The nerves of Dushanbe's war-weary population are jangled every few minutes as anonymous youngsters drop firecrackers in the streets.
"It's done by the opposition, they're clever as it confuses the security forces' reactions," said the Russian officer.
Patrolled by armoured vehicles, the streets empty quickly when darkness falls.

With the guerrillas apparently able to strike at will, diplomats fear an Algerian-style terror campaign in Dushanbe. "It would be easy for them to do -- the question is why don't they?" said the diplomat.

Observers say the main reason for opposition hesitancy is Russian armour. Fearing Islamic fundamentalism near its vulnerable southern border, Russia has 20,000-odd border guards and motorised infantry stationed in the former Soviet colony who wield enormous influence.

Underlying the civil war are seething regional and clan rivalries and a battle for control of the impoverished republic's few remaining riches -- some gold, fast declining cotton production and narcotics.
Rakhmonov's clan from the southern Kulyab region now holds the purse strings.
"There is corruption and high prices. They just take the cotton and pay us nothing, this isn't a state," said opposition field commander Rakhmon Sanginov.
Rakhmonov survived a military mutiny last February when discontent with the Kulyab clan's influence reached boiling point.
"The Kulyabis are terribly unpopular," said the diplomat. "Flaunting their wealth as they do, they're clearly going to do themselves in sooner or later."
